content: In the second stage of labor, fetal heart rate (FHR) monitoring is recommended before the mother begins bearing down and every five minutes during active pushing. A trial conducted in Zimbabwe involving 633 women compared four methods of FHR monitoring: intermittent cardiotocography (CTG), Doppler ultrasound, and two Pinard fetal stethoscope methods (strict and routine practice). In the CTG group, an external transducer was applied for 10 minutes every 30 minutes to monitor FHR, though the consistency of contraction monitoring was unclear. The Doppler and strict Pinard methods involved a research midwife auscultating the FHR for one minute during the last 10 minutes of every half-hour, both during and after a contraction. In the routine Pinard group, midwives performed auscultation as part of standard care. Participants in the Zimbabwe trial had obstetric or medical risk factors (excluding placental abruption or eclampsia) and were either booked or transferred to a referral hospital for childbirth. The evidence from this trial was downgraded for indirectness when included in meta-analyses. All participants had term singleton pregnancies with cephalic presentation, cervical dilation ≤7 cm, and FHR between 120–160 beats per minute upon admission. Comparison 1: Doppler Ultrasound vs. Routine Pinard Stethoscope Data from trials in Uganda and Zimbabwe contributed to this comparison. Evidence on the effect of these methods on overall cesarean section rates was of very low certainty. No evidence was available regarding maternal childbirth experience, including satisfaction, preferred labor positions, or perceived control. The absolute difference in hypoxic-ischemic encephalopathy (HIE) was estimated at 29 fewer cases per 1,000 births (range: 7–31 fewer). Evidence on Apgar scores was of very low certainty, and long-term infant outcomes were not reported. Doppler monitoring in lowand middle-income countries (LMICs) may increase detection of FHR abnormalities and subsequent cesarean sections for fetal distress, potentially reducing perinatal hypoxia-ischemia. However, it remains uncertain whether these benefits translate to improved long-term infant outcomes. No research evidence on the relative costs or cost-effectiveness of Doppler versus Pinard was found. Comparison 2: Intermittent CTG vs. Routine Pinard Stethoscope Evidence for this comparison came from the Zimbabwe trial involving 633 women. The routine Pinard group received standard care from midwives. Participants were women with risk factors for complications, and the evidence was downgraded for indirectness. No evidence was available on maternal birth experience, including satisfaction, preferred labor positions, or perceived control. The absolute difference in HIE was estimated at 25 fewer cases per 1,000 births (range: 3–30 fewer). Evidence on Apgar scores <7 at five minutes was of very low certainty, and cord blood acidosis was not reported. The absolute difference in detecting early and late decelerations was estimated at 134 more cases per 1,000 births (range: 60–252 more). It remains uncertain whether increased detection of decelerations and cesarean sections for fetal distress improved early or long-term infant outcomes. Women generally desire normal childbirth with good outcomes for both mother and baby but acknowledge that interventions may sometimes be necessary. When interventions are considered, women prefer to be informed and given a choice. Intermittent CTG in LMICs may increase detection of FHR abnormalities and reduce perinatal hypoxia-ischemia at the expense of increased cesarean sections for fetal distress. However, CTG may reduce equity if it leads to a cascade of interventions affordable only to advantaged women in well-resourced settings. Comparison 3: Strict vs. Routine Pinard Monitoring This comparison was based on the Zimbabwe trial involving 625 women with risk factors for complications. Evidence was downgraded for indirectness. No evidence was available on maternal birth experience, including satisfaction, preferred labor positions, or perceived control. Evidence on Apgar scores <7 at five minutes, neonatal seizures, and HIE was of very low certainty. It remains uncertain whether increased identification of FHR abnormalities leads to improved birth and long-term infant outcomes. Women may appreciate the more intimate connection with healthcare providers enabled by strict monitoring, provided it is conducted by kind, competent staff sensitive to their needs. Healthcare professionals also prefer delivering woman-centered care if sufficient resources are available to support the labor-intensive nature of this approach. Strict monitoring may be more resource-intensive in terms of staff time. Epidural Analgesia for Pain Relief Epidural analgesia is recommended for healthy pregnant women requesting pain relief during labor, depending on their preferences. While evidence on its impact compared to no epidural is limited, epidural analgesia is a proven method for relieving surgical pain and is recommended as a labor pain relief option. Women’s desire for epidural analgesia may be influenced by the clinical context, type of care, and access to other pain relief options. Epidural analgesia is more effective than opioids but requires more resources and has more common adverse effects. To minimize complications and preserve motor function, the lowest effective concentration of local anesthetic should be used. Women with epidural analgesia in the second stage of labor should be supported in their choice of birth position, including upright positions, and pushing may be delayed until the sensory urge to bear down returns. Summary The choice of FHR monitoring and pain relief methods during labor should consider maternal and fetal outcomes, resource availability, and women’s preferences. While advanced technologies like Doppler and CTG may improve detection of FHR abnormalities, their cost and feasibility in low-resource settings remain challenges. Similarly, epidural analgesia offers effective pain relief but requires significant resources and careful management of adverse effects. Women value informed decision-making, competent care, and interventions that prioritize the well-being of both mother and baby.
